Again, this is explanation not endorsement. Maybe "richer" was the wrong term, but certainly more varied. Having a kid becomes an easier proposition when your life is very routine and you can see where a child would fit in. When the things you enjoy are expensive and logistically difficult, having a kid is more disruptive, and today's young people do things like travel and dine out much more than their parents (they're also likely to live in cities which tend to be expensive). You don't have to

I didn't say that today's young people are HAPPIER or feel that their lives are more meaningful. But I would guess that more of them believe they should derive meaning from their jobs. I would guess that their lives are more varied compared to, say, the lives of the average Boomer. And that they live in a way that they rightly assess would be disrupted by children. That's not me arguing that they shouldn't have children, it's me saying that they look at their lives and decide it's impossible not

I'm genuinely confused by people who say this is the opposite of true. How many Baby Boomers were traveling the world in their 20s the way today's college-educated gainfully employed 20-somethings travel? How many spent their 20s (and often 30s) in big cities, eating out at restaurants, going out with friends, and so on? I'm not saying no one did this before, but I am saying that young people spend more of their income on experiences like travel, dining, etc, which suggests to me that they're pr

I remain convinced that virtually no one actually forgoes having children because of climate change. People who want kids but are concerned about the climate justify having them. People who don’t want kids feel they need a noble-sounding reason and climate change is a great one.


Billy Binion (@billybinion)

From the author of the new NYT story on why some people aren't having kids. People should do what's best for them, but I find it extremely sad that anyone would forgo having a family becaus

I think an under appreciated part of the birth rate discourse is that many more young people simply have richer and more textured lives than young people in previous generations: hobbies, travel, meaningful jobs, deep friendships. Children present more possible disruption than they did a generation or two ago.

Justin Brannan (@JustinBrannan)

Caputo’s Bakery on Court Street, a.k.a. “the bread store,” has unexpectedly closed after 124 YEARS! They were a fifth-generation, family-run bakery for all that time. We’re all gonna need some time (and a seeded twist) to mourn this one.









— https://nitter.net/JustinBrannan/status/2048957538268332175#m
Call me when the NYT is ready for a "12 Bitches Who Were Right about Everything" piece.

I truly think we've made something special. So if this sounds like something you might like, I hope you take the leap and sign up. Full disclosure it's mostly women. Most come alone, some bring a friend. But you can come as you are, whoever you are, with whoever you want to come with.

Retreats are very very very fun and I hope you'll consider joining me! Not to toot my own horn too loudly but ever since my collaborator Emily and I hosted our first retreat together we've had multiple repeat retreaters return on every single retreat, and at this point we've done at least a dozen.

Imagine taking a week to have all of your needs met: someone offering you creative practice, someone offering you movement practice, dinner reservations made, interesting people around the table, wine poured on when you arrive. Space to make and move and be. onthegroundretreats.com/retreat/greece

I host writing and yoga retreats around the world. And no, "go on a yoga retreat" is not the answer to society-wide loneliness or burnout or any Big Huge Problems. But it is one way to give yourself a damn break. To have fun. To exhale. onthegroundretreats.com/retreat/greece

We hear a lot about loneliness epidemics, too much stress, too much time on screens, too little time with other people, too much work and not enough creation. One antidote: Travel to a magical place with a small group of people. Write. Move your body. Make lasting friendships.

By @jillfilipovic.bsky.social 

GIFT article.
"The old anti-abortion movement strategy was to attack contraception as immoral, though few Americans share that view. The new tactic is more MAHA-coded, and with a #pronatalist twist:" 1/2

This is a gift link!

The same reason they push viagra like dealers.

I talked with the iconic Jessica Yellin about the authoritarian impulse to target women, from ICE enforcement to Russia to Trump's America to the just-toppled Hungarian regime: 
newsnotnoisejessicayellin.substack.com/p/the-patter...

The Trump administration wants to take money that has long paid for modern contraception for low-income women and spend it on helping sperm swim better. This is not a joke. 
www.nytimes.com/2026/04/20/o...
"The guy ran for president! And still, when presented with an attractive woman on social media, he seems to have thought the appropriate response was, “Here, look, this is my penis""
“The impulse to send them seems to stem not from a desire to seduce but to subordinate-less mating dance than dominance ritual, a way to push a woman's boundaries and see what she'll tolerate.”
Thank you! It is all... very strange.

A huge amount of this is that there's still an unspoken but heavily enforced social norm that women are obliged to keep men's dirty secrets, whether you consented or not. 

The second a man assaults or harasses you, he invokes this unspoken contract.

There's been a sharp uptick in religiosity among young men. I think I know why.
